newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: NSW police corruption endemic - Wood report.
newsitem.headline: NSW police corruption endemic - Wood report.

text.p: Police corruption is systematic and entrenched in Australia's largest force, similar to the New York Police Department in 1994, with police involved in the drugs trade and competing with criminals to commit crimes.
An official report into corruption in the New South Wales Police Force released on Thursday said the force has "rarely been free of corruption" in its history.

"Perhaps the most disturbing of all was the extent to which police admitted to being directly involved in the supply of cocaine, heroin and cannibis," said Supreme Court Judge James Wood in his three-volume report.

In one incident a drug dealer provided police with A$12,000 to finance a "buy-bust". The drugs, two ounces of heroin, were seized by police, but the money "lost" in the raid. Later the police divided the drugs up with the dealer.
Police were also involved in theft and extortion, took bribes to protect drug dealers and bookmakers, lied in court to ensure prosecution and assaulted and arrested innocent people.
"On any view of the inquiries of the royal commission disclosed a very serious state of corruption that was widespread and of long-standing origin," Wood said.
"The culture was such, and the management and internal investigative systems were so deficient, that the state of corruption found can only be regarded as systematic and entrenched," he said.
"The service has rarely been free of corruption."

Wood said the rise of drug crime in the past 20 years significantly increased police corruption, exposing more police to the "temptations of easy money", and expanding corruption from the traditional areas such as gambling and alcohol.

"What is of concern...is the active involvement of police in planning and implementing criminal activity, sometimes in partnership with known criminals, and on other occassions, in competition with them," Wood said.

"This finding mirrors the experience of the 1994 Molen Inquiry which similarly found that corruption within the New York Police Department was no longer confined to fortuitous opportunity...but often arose because police created and actively planned similar activities."

Wood said that corruption occured because of "rotten apples", a police culture called the "brotherhood" where police put up a code of silence to protect each other, and because policing and corruption "go hand in hand".
"The simple fact is that corruption does not emrege suddenly. By its nature it is spawned in stealth and grows in a climate in which it is comfortable."
Wood said that unless fundamental changes in the culture and operation of New South Wales Police Force were implemented then corruption would continue.

Wood recommended random field inspections of police operations, greater use of uniformed police in investigations, the use of tape recorders for police interviews, proper management of informants and a move towards the decriminalisation of heroin use.
During his two-year corruption inquiry, Wood offered corrupt police an amnesty if they agreed to testify.
A series of undercover operations by the inquiry saw corrupt police video-taped taking bribes and dealing in drugs with prostitutes.

The New South Wales state government in February agreed to implement recommendations from Wood's interim report, such as creating a new all-powerful anti-corruption body, which will have the power to bug telephones and have access to all police files.
